1215.bp: Depression is a crushing public health crisis—it crushes individuals and overloads the few mental health professionals available. Most people never talk to a doctor about it; instead they confess online in forums, Reddit, subreddits, social media. If we could read these raw confessions and automatically spot the telltale signs of depression, we could flag people who need help and lift some load off scarce clinicians.
1215.wh: The problem is that depression doesn't announce itself the same way each person expresses it. The clinical definition of depression has 21 distinct symptoms—sadness, loss of appetite, sleep problems, guilt, concentration trouble, and so on. A single sentence "I haven't eaten in days" is crystal-clear evidence of appetite loss. But "I've been staying in bed" could mean appetite loss, fatigue, loss of interest, or something else entirely. Most LLM systems either try to answer with zero examples, learn from a few in-context examples, or are fine-tuned, but they all struggle because the imbalance is extreme—guilt and shame come up constantly; suicidal ideation almost never—and the criteria for what counts as evidence drift across different doctors' training data.
1215.ap: The researchers created a dataset called BDI-Sen, where humans labeled sentences from online text with which of the 21 symptoms they show evidence of. Then they built Symptom Induction: instead of asking the LLM to classify directly, they feed it a small set of labeled examples and ask it to write out a short, plain-English summary of "what counts as evidence of this symptom." Those summaries become reusable guidelines that condition every classification decision afterward.
1215.ww: This works because LLMs are extraordinarily good at squeezing complex patterns into brief, interpretable rules. The guidelines act as a shared contract: "fatigue is when someone reports extreme tiredness, inability to move, or constant sleepiness," full stop. By making the criteria explicit and consistent, the LLM doesn't have to reinvent its decision threshold for every new example. The guidelines also generalize—a rule for "guilt" in depression often captures similar guilt in bipolar disorder or eating disorders, so the same approach works across different diseases.
1215.po: Across eight different LLM models, this approach consistently beats zero-shot, in-context learning, and standard fine-tuning. The biggest wins come on rare symptoms where the dataset has almost no examples—the guidelines help the model generalize from scarce evidence. On an external test set covering bipolar and eating disorders, the induced guidelines still perform well, showing that the approach doesn't overfit to depression.

1216.bp: Real-world networks are alive—they change by the hour. Social networks pulse with new users joining and old accounts dormant; cryptocurrencies flow between wallets; message graphs expand with every conversation. Within these churning networks, fraud and abuse happens silently: a bot army suddenly coordinates, money laundering accelerates, suspicious accounts wake up and disappear. Detecting these anomalies without labeled training data is the goal—you can't afford to label every node as normal or malicious when the network shifts faster than your annotations.
1216.wh: The dilemma is that anomalies are rare and weird—they don't repeat in the same way. A local detector might spot an isolated node that suddenly explodes with activity, but miss a coordinated ring of actors far away who look normal individually. A global detector remembers that "globally similar behavior is usually normal," but applying that requires labeled data to know what normal is. And there's a causality trap: if you're trying to detect fraud at time T, you can't peek at messages that haven't arrived yet—you can only use the past.
1216.ap: The method, DGRA-CL, works in layers. First, it treats the dynamic network as a sequence of time steps and learns what "normal behavior" looks like using an unsupervised technique called self-learning—pairs of similar nodes are pushed close together, dissimilar ones pushed apart, all without labels. Second, it retrieves from memory: for any node at time T, it digs through the pool of historical normal nodes and finds the closest matches, but crucially, only using data from times before T (strict causality). Third, it blends: it constructs a "baseline normal pattern" by averaging the retrieved neighbors, weighted by how similar they are. Finally, it scores: any node that deviates sharply from its baseline is flagged as anomalous.
1216.ww: This cascade works because normal behavior tends to cluster—most users just chat normally, most transactions are routine. By learning to recognize normal patterns globally while respecting causality, the detector can spot both isolated weirdness and coordinated rings. The retrieval step ensures you're comparing each node to truly similar peers, not to the entire network, which dramatically sharpens the detection.
1216.po: On real networks (message graphs, Bitcoin transactions, social platforms), the method gains 1-2 percentage points in detection accuracy (AUC) over the best prior methods on most benchmarks. Those small-sounding gains matter hugely at scale—even 1% more anomalies caught in a billion-node network is massive fraud prevented.

1217.bp: Personalized learning is the dream: adapt the lesson difficulty, pacing, and content to what each student actually knows. To do that, a system needs to constantly infer each student's knowledge state—which algebra concepts they've mastered, which they're foggy on, which they haven't seen yet. This inference only works if you have data on what each student did; but many students generate very little data—a few quiz attempts, skipping most lessons. How do you reliably guess a student's knowledge when you have almost no signal?
1217.wh: The bottleneck is sparsity. Traditional knowledge-tracing systems (systems that track what students know) fine-tune themselves on individual students' history. If a student has only 20 interactions, that's too little signal to distinguish "they forgot this skill" from "they never learned it." Prior work tried self-supervised learning: take one student's sequence, artificially shuffle or crop parts of it, and train the model to match the two versions. The problem is that synthetic augmentations are noise—shuffling events doesn't capture real learning, and the model only sees this one student's trajectory.
1217.ap: This paper (RACL) flips the strategy: instead of comparing a student to fake versions of themselves, compare real students to each other. The key insight is that students with similar skill profiles—one student who's strong in arithmetic but weak in fractions, another who matches that profile—often exhibit comparable learning trajectories. So you construct positive examples by finding naturally similar students and using their real sequences as signals. Negative examples are naturally dissimilar students. The system learns to represent each student's trajectory in a space where similar learners cluster.
1217.ww: This is powerful because genuine pedagogical similarity is far richer than synthetic augmentation. Two real students who both struggled with variables and then conquered it are a stronger signal than one student's artificially shuffled sequence. The system essentially borrows strength from similar peers—if a sparse student's trajectory looks like a well-tracked peer who's similar, the model can infer knowledge more confidently.
1217.po: On four benchmarks, the method improves accuracy by 1.2% on average over prior methods. More crucially, when trained on only 20% of the data (simulating very sparse students), it retains 97% of its normal accuracy, whereas competitors degrade sharply. This means the method enables effective personalization for students who otherwise wouldn't generate enough data.

1218.bp: Recommender systems rank items for users—which movie, article, product to show first. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly good at ranking because they can reason about nuanced preferences from free text. But LLMs process sequences one token at a time, left to right. If you present items in one order, the model might rate them differently than if you shuffle them—even though logically, the set of items hasn't changed. This inconsistency is a nightmare: your top-ranked movie might only rank high because it happened to come second in the prompt, not because it's actually best.
1218.wh: The problem is architectural. LLMs have something called positional encoding—they track where each word is in the sequence so they know context. When you list items [Item A, Item B, Item C], the model uses position information plus the item descriptions to score each one. Permute to [Item B, Item A, Item C] and the positions change, the model's reasoning changes slightly, and the scores shift. This is order sensitivity, and it's not a small bug—it violates the core principle that recommendations should depend on preferences, not on how you happened to arrange the prompt.
1218.ap: InvariRank addresses this at the architectural level. It uses two tricks. First, it modifies the attention mechanism—the part of the LLM that lets each item "see" other items—to block cross-item attention. This prevents the score of one item from being influenced by another item's position. Second, it uses a special positional encoding called Rotary Positional Embeddings that has a mathematical property: when combined with the structured attention mask, it effectively makes position irrelevant to scoring. All items are scored in a single forward pass, not in multiple permutations.
1218.ww: Blocking cross-item attention means each item's score depends only on the item itself and the query, not on what other items surround it. Combined with rotation-invariant positional encoding, this ensures that shuffling items doesn't change their scores. It's pure mathematics: the rotation properties of RoPE interact with the blocked attention to cancel out position dependence.
1218.po: On recommendation benchmarks, InvariRank maintains competitive ranking accuracy—it doesn't sacrifice quality. More importantly, it produces stable rankings: shuffle the candidate set ten different ways and the relative rankings stay identical. Crucially, it does this in one forward pass, no permutation tricks, so it's also faster and more practical than methods that require re-ranking the same set multiple times.

1219.bp: Search engines need to answer queries instantly—you type and expect results in milliseconds. Modern search uses dense embeddings, which are compact learned representations of text—think of each document as a point in a high-dimensional space. When you search, your query becomes a point too, and the system finds nearby points (similar documents). This is fast and accurate, but computing and storing millions of high-dimensional points is expensive. Under heavy load—when thousands of queries hit simultaneously—the system might bottleneck: does it serve queries slowly, or drop some entirely?
1219.wh: The tension is load-dependent: when traffic is light, you want maximum accuracy, so full-resolution embeddings shine. When traffic is heavy, you need to cut costs and avoid timeouts. But most systems use fixed-resolution embeddings year-round. You either overtune for peak load (wasting compute under normal load) or undersize for peak (and drop queries during surges). The naive fix—always use smaller embeddings—hurts accuracy. The catch is timing: you can't predict when the next surge hits or how long it lasts.
1219.ap: This paper proposes a load-sensitive approach: monitor the query queue in real time. If queries are piling up (high queue depth) or if a query has a deadline approaching, adaptively shrink the embedding dimensionality on the fly. For example, use 768-dimensional embeddings when queues are empty, but drop to 128 dimensions when the queue fills. They test two dimensionality-reduction strategies: PCA (classical linear compression) and Matryoshka embeddings (a learned multi-scale representation). Both can be applied dynamically at inference time without retraining.
1219.ww: This works because embedding quality degrades gracefully with dimension. A 256-dimensional embedding is much smaller than 768 but still captures most of the information—you lose some nuance but keep the broad strokes. By tracking queue depth and query deadlines, you're making a real-time speed vs. accuracy trade-off that matches actual system pressure. When the system is quiet, you're not penalizing users with worse results.
1219.po: Empirically, the load-aware approach beats static dimensionality reduction across varying loads. Interestingly, the paper also shows that PCA-based compression outperforms Matryoshka embeddings when used with this adaptive strategy, suggesting that simpler compression is sufficient when you're already adapting to load. The practical payoff is consistent effectiveness-to-efficiency trade-offs—no need to manually tune for average, worst-case, or typical load.

1220.bp: Search systems sometimes use clustering to organize documents into groups, which makes large-scale retrieval faster—instead of searching 8 million documents, you search a few cluster centers first, then drill into the top clusters. The question is how to partition 8 million documents into, say, 100,000 clusters efficiently. K-means, the classical clustering method, works well conceptually but becomes glacially slow when you have hundreds of thousands of clusters. This paper revisits an old-school partitioning method and tweaks it to handle massive document sets.
1220.wh: K-means is simple: you pick K cluster centers, assign each point to the nearest center, then move the centers and repeat. But when K is large (say, 100K), each iteration touches every point and every center, so you're doing massive matrix multiplications over and over. On 8 million documents, this is prohibitively slow. Bipartite graph partitioning (BP) is a classical alternative that recursively splits documents in half, which scales logarithmically—you do log(K) splits, each roughly linear in the number of documents. But BP doesn't use K-means, so it might cluster differently.
1220.ap: The paper proposes a hybrid: K-means-guided bisection. Instead of running full K-means with K clusters, you recursively bisect (split in two) while using K-means principles to guide each split. At each step, you find the split that best mirrors what K-means would prefer, but you only do one bisection at a time. After log(K) splits, you've partitioned documents into K groups with K-means-like quality but logarithmic time complexity instead of linear-per-iteration.
1220.ww: Bisection is mathematically efficient: every partition doubles the number of clusters, so you need only log₂(K) steps. By guiding each bisection with K-means logic, you keep the clustering quality high without paying K-means' full cost. The recursive structure also means earlier bisections can be parallelized independent of later ones.
1220.po: On real document sets (8.8 million passages from MS MARCO), the method is 29–414× faster than K-means variants and reduces final retrieval latency by up to 32% compared to basic bipartite partitioning. So you get both speed and better clustering quality than prior alternatives.

1221.bp: Neural retrieval systems learn to rank documents by searching through massive collections and returning the most relevant ones. The quality of results depends heavily on preprocessing: how you clean up text, tokenize it, chunk it into passages, augment it with synonyms—dozens of small choices. Most teams hand-craft a preprocessing pipeline once and use it for all datasets. But different datasets (scientific papers vs. news articles vs. short tweets) need different preprocessing. Ideally, you'd customize preprocessing per dataset, but trying 700 different pipelines by hand is infeasible.
1221.wh: The trap is that preprocessing and neural retrieval are usually treated as separate: first you preprocess, then you train the retriever. This means preprocessing choices are fixed before you even know how the neural model will respond to them. It's like tuning the engine and transmission in separate buildings—you lose the opportunity to optimize them together. Additionally, there are 700 possible preprocessing configurations (choices about cleaning, tokenization, chunking, augmentation), and trying them all by brute force would take forever.
1221.ap: PrepRet reformulates preprocessing selection as a differentiable optimization problem. Instead of trying configurations one at a time, the system represents each choice (e.g., "should we apply lowercase? yes or no?") as a soft, learnable parameter. These parameters are adjusted using gradient descent—the same mechanism that trains neural models. A hierarchical mechanism captures dependencies between preprocessing stages, so the system can learn that if you lowercase, you shouldn't apply a stemmer (they conflict). The gradient-based search explores the space of 700 configurations efficiently, taking only 1.1 GPU-hours.
1221.ww: Gradient-based optimization is exponentially faster than brute force because it follows the signal—it learns which preprocessing choices help or hurt the final ranking quality. The hierarchy captures that preprocessing isn't a bag of independent choices; operations in sequence build on each other, and the system learns those dependencies.
1221.po: On MS MARCO, the learned pipeline achieves 0.533 nDCG@10 (a ranking quality metric), beating hand-crafted baselines by 7.7% and a strong pretrained retriever (Contriever) by 11.7%. When tested zero-shot on eight other domains (scientific papers, medical text, entity-rich queries), it generalizes well, with especially strong gains on specialized domains. This means one learned preprocessing pipeline adapts across datasets.

1222.bp: Recommendation systems learn from implicit feedback: clicks, purchases, watches. But not every click means "I liked this"—sometimes you misclick, sometimes you buy something that disappoints, sometimes you accidentally view an item. These false positives are noise that corrupts the training signal. If you naively treat all clicks as positive preferences, the model learns misleading patterns. Most denoising methods try to filter out suspicious (high-loss) samples, but this creates a trade-off: by penalizing high-loss samples, you also weaken the signal on hard-to-learn true positives.
1222.wh: The core tension is ambiguity. When a sample has high loss during training, it could mean two things: the model is struggling to learn a genuinely hard true positive, or it's encountering a noisy false positive. Standard denoising methods can't distinguish—they just downweight high-loss samples indiscriminately. This breaks learning on hard but real preferences. The implicit feedback problem is fundamentally a labeling uncertainty problem: for each click, the true label might be "user liked it" or "user didn't like it," and you don't know which.
1222.ap: PLLD reformulates the denoising problem through the lens of partial label learning (PLL). In PLL, for each sample, you know the true label is somewhere in a candidate set (maybe it's positive OR negative, but you don't know which). Treated this way, denoising becomes label disambiguation: for each high-loss sample, the system learns to decide which label in the candidate set is most likely correct. Instead of heuristically filtering samples, it directly resolves the ambiguity using PLL techniques.
1222.ww: PLL is designed exactly for this setting: when you have multiple possible labels per sample and need to find the true one. By treating implicit feedback as a PLL problem, the system can learn to distinguish true positives (clicks that reflect genuine preference) from false positives (misclicks) without throwing away hard examples. The PLL machinery ensures you keep learning from hard true positives while filtering noisy ones.
1222.po: On recommendation benchmarks, PLLD outperforms existing denoising methods by more robustly recovering clean signals from noisy implicit feedback. The method is especially effective when feedback is sparse or when the noise rate is high—situations where naive filtering methods historically fail.

1223.bp: Large language models are increasingly used to rerank search results—you get a rough set of candidates from a fast retriever, then use an LLM to score them more carefully. LLMs are good at this because they understand nuance and context. But adapting an LLM to a specialized domain (e.g., medical literature, legal documents) requires collecting and annotating domain-specific training data, which is expensive and time-consuming. Task vectors offer a shortcut: they capture domain-specific knowledge learned during training and can be transplanted into a model.
1223.wh: Task vectors are derived from continuous pretraining—they encode the knowledge an LLM picked up while learning domain-specific text. But applying task vectors to a model is tricky: you can't just add them (too aggressive), and scaling them is sensitive to tuning the scale factor. Use too small a scale, and you get weak domain adaptation. Use too large a scale, and you degrade the LLM's core ranking ability or even confuse its behavior across domains. There's no one-size-fits-all scaling factor.
1223.ap: The method learns parameter-wise scaling: instead of a single scale factor, the system learns a separate scale for each parameter in the task vector. These scales are optimized using a language modeling loss—the system just needs to continue predicting text, not to label retrieval examples. All model parameters are frozen, so only the scales are learned, which is fast and computationally cheap.
1223.ww: Parameter-wise scaling is more expressive than a global scale. Some parts of the task vector might transfer cleanly to reranking (e.g., domain terminology), while others might not (e.g., generation style from pretraining). By learning per-parameter scales, the system automatically learns which parts to integrate fully, which to dampen, and which to ignore. The language modeling loss is a stable training signal that doesn't require domain-specific labeled data.
1223.po: On a general-domain benchmark and five specialized domains, the method provides stable improvements across most domains without the performance degradation seen with fixed scaling. On larger and smaller model scales, the method consistently helps, showing that it generalizes across model sizes. The approach is practical: you need only unlabeled domain text and a small amount of compute to adapt an LLM reranker to a new domain.

1224.bp: Recommendation systems use embeddings—learned vectors that represent users and items in a shared space, where similar users and items are close together. Recently, systems have started refining pre-trained embeddings after initial training to improve recommendation quality. But current methods only refine item embeddings, leaving user embeddings alone. This asymmetry breaks the alignment between the two types of embeddings, like tuning one speaker of a stereo but leaving the other as is.
1224.wh: User and item embeddings are jointly trained under a low-rank assumption—roughly, their interactions can be modeled by multiplying user and item vectors. Refining only items disrupts this alignment: the refined items are optimized for the original user vectors, which were trained differently. The embedding space becomes distorted, and the system ends up recommending a narrower range of items (bad for diversity) or misses good matches (bad for accuracy).
1224.ap: REFORM reformulates post-training refinement as a matrix factorization problem. The system constructs a target matrix that incorporates two objectives: preserving the angular structure of pre-trained embeddings (which reliably encodes which users prefer which items, regardless of popularity) and incorporating frequency signals (recent items and popular items carry more confidence). It then jointly refactorizes the user and item embeddings to match this target, keeping both aligned.
1224.ww: By treating refinement as factorization, the system naturally keeps user and item embeddings in sync—they're jointly learning to match the target matrix. The angular structure preservation ensures that the refined embeddings don't throw away hard-earned preference knowledge from pretraining. Frequency signals let the system incorporate recent data without overweighting rare items.
1224.po: On three benchmark datasets, REFORM gains up to 26.9% in recall and 29.2% in NDCG (ranking quality metrics) over post-training baselines. Crucially, it maintains higher effective rank—the embeddings continue to represent a wider diversity of items—and better item coverage, so users see more varied recommendations. This solves a long-standing trade-off between accuracy and diversity.

1225.bp: Sequential recommenders predict what a user will interact with next by looking at their history—if you watched action movies, then comedies, then action again, the system infers you're in an action mood. But in real systems, there's a lag: interactions are logged asynchronously, so when the model makes a prediction, it hasn't seen the user's most recent actions yet. If someone clicked three items in the last hour but those clicks take 30 minutes to appear in the log, the model's decision is based on a stale, incomplete history.
1225.wh: The problem is temporal misalignment. Traditional sequential models assume they see the true, immediately observed sequence of actions. But with delayed logging, the visible sequence is censored—some recent real actions are missing. The model thinks the user's trajectory ended an hour ago, when actually they've continued interacting. This causes the model to make outdated predictions or miss trends in progress. Different delays (5 minutes vs. 1 hour) affect different parts of the user's history differently, compounding the confusion.
1225.ap: DVGD models user-item interactions as a dynamic graph and learns to route information across multiple time lags. The key insight is decoupling: separate out which features matter (feature-wise dependencies) from how those features change over time (temporal dependencies). The system learns a time-lag adjacency tensor—essentially, for each possible delay, it learns how to weight historical connections. When making a prediction, it accounts for the fact that some recent data might be missing.
1225.ww: By explicitly modeling lag, the system learns that recent censored data (missing actions) follows predictable patterns from the history it does see. If you saw someone click home goods, then nothing, then the model knows recent clicks probably clustered around that interest. The variate-temporal decomposition lets the system learn feature-specific and time-specific patterns independently, making the lag-modeling more flexible.
1225.po: On benchmarks with controlled, simulated delays, the method consistently beats baselines, with larger gains when delays are longer or vary wildly. While validation on real delayed logs is pending, the method shows promise for deploying sequential recommenders in real-world systems with latency.

1226.bp: Entity linking is the task of tying mentions of things to their definitions—when you read "Paris" in an article, is it the French city or Paris Hilton? With images, the problem is richer: an image of a person or object might show their Wikipedia article, if you could recognize them. Multimodal entity linking combines text and image signals to identify entities. In practice (product catalogs, news archives, social media), these systems need to work at scale: millions of entities, millions of lookups per day, which means both speed and storage matter.
1226.wh: Current state-of-the-art methods encode text and images separately into high-dimensional vectors, then search for the closest match in the knowledge base. This is accurate but slow and memory-hungry: encoding each entity takes time, storing millions of high-dimensional vectors consumes gigabytes. There's a speed-memory-accuracy triangle: current methods pick two (e.g., fast and accurate but storage-heavy, or compact but slow).
1226.ap: FAST-MEL uses a lightweight encoder that produces a compact fixed-size representation for each entity and mention, combining both text and visual information into a single vector. The key is making the representation small enough to store efficiently but rich enough to preserve matching accuracy. The system then uses these compact representations to match mentions to entities.
1226.ww: Compact representations save storage (one order of magnitude less than competitors) and reduce computational cost. By merging text and image information early into a unified vector, the system avoids redundant encoding and can perform lookups rapidly. The careful design of the representation ensures that similarity is preserved despite the compression.
1226.po: The method matches the accuracy of the best existing systems while being three orders of magnitude faster (faster by 1000×) and consuming one order of magnitude less storage. This is a rare win-win: you get speed, accuracy, and storage efficiency simultaneously, making the system practical for large-scale deployment.

1227.bp: Large language models are increasingly used to evaluate search results and question-answering systems, especially in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipelines where the system finds documents and generates answers from them. Automated LLM evaluation works by checking whether an answer covers all the key facts (nuggets) that should be present. The challenge is constructing a good nugget bank: the set of facts that the answer should address. A bank that's too small might miss important details; too large and evaluation becomes prohibitively expensive (hundreds of LLM calls per answer).
1227.wh: Nuggets are currently constructed by combining human insight and LLM generation, but the result is often bloated with generic questions that don't distinguish between good and great answers. For example, "Does the answer mention the location?" applies to almost every domain and fails to catch subtle quality differences. Grounding nuggets in actual system outputs helps (asking more specific things), but this creates an explosion—instead of 20 nuggets, you need 100, which increases evaluation cost tenfold.
1227.ap: The paper proposes deriving nuggets from contrastive pairs: when comparing two systems' outputs, which one is better? The nuggets should capture the differences between top-performing systems. The system looks at winner-loser pairs and extracts nuggets that capture differences in topicality, detail level, and evidence quality. These nuggets are naturally specific (since they reflect real system differences) yet sparse (since they only capture what actually differs between systems).
1227.wh: This works because contrastive signals are high-signal. If system A beat system B on a particular query, the differentiating factor is often something specific—more relevant sources, more detail, better evidence. By grounding nuggets in these real differences, the system generates nuggets that are both discriminative (they separate good from mediocre) and concise. You get fewer nuggets but with higher utility.
1227.po: The resulting nugget banks are both compact and discriminative, enabling reliable evaluation of RAG systems while keeping the cost reasonable. Because nuggets are derived from actual system behaviors, they naturally scale with system quality—improving systems generate new meaningful differentiators for future evaluation.

1228.bp: Conversational search lets people refine information needs through dialogue—instead of crafting a single query, you chat with the system, ask follow-ups, and correct misunderstandings. But incorporating personal preferences into ranking remains hard. Some preferences are explicit ("show me cheaper options"), others implicit (you hate clickbait). Traditional reranking looks at topical relevance but not user constraints, so good documents get hidden if they don't match formatting preferences or run counter to stated dislikes.
1228.wh: The difficulty is that instructions for personalized search are buried in the conversation and user profile—they're implicit, not written out. Plus, different queries need different levels of personalization. A simple query like "hotels in Paris" just needs straightforward ranking, but a complex query with multiple constraints ("under 100 euros, no shared bath, near metro, good reviews") needs careful instruction-following. Standard approaches apply the same reranking method to all queries, which adds latency and noise on simple queries.
1228.ap: APR (Adaptive Personalised Reranking) routes queries based on complexity. For simple queries, it uses fast, basic reranking. For complex or constraint-heavy queries, it generates tailored instructions by reading the user's history and profile ("this user prefers boutique hotels", "this user has a tight budget"), then uses an instruction-following reranker to score documents against those instructions. The routing decision is learned, so the system automatically learns which queries benefit from instruction-following.
1228.ww: Routing is efficient: you only pay the cost of instruction-following for queries that need it. For simple queries, you skip the overhead. The generated instructions are grounded in user data, making them personal rather than generic. An instruction-following model can enforce complex, multi-faceted constraints (price, format, style, sentiment) in ways that topic-only ranking can't.
1228.po: On TREC conversational search benchmarks, APR shows that instruction-following acts as a "rescue" mechanism for hard queries—it prevents failures on complex requests. When trained with synthetic data (no hand-annotated conversational preferences), APR competes with strong baselines like MonoT5 while opening new research directions. The method is practical and runs at conversational speeds.

1229.bp: Online travel platforms (booking sites) face a multistage buying process: first, you scan a list of hotels and click on one that catches your eye. Then, inside that hotel's page, you see rooms of different types and prices and choose one to book. Pricing decisions are tightly coupled: if you reduce the price of the deluxe room, some customers will upgrade from standard; lower the suite price and some will downgrade. Accurately predicting demand and setting prices requires understanding this substitution effect—how changes in one product's price ripple through a set.
1229.wh: Most current methods collapse this into a single stage (just predict booking or not) and ignore substitution effects entirely. This creates biased demand estimates because they don't account for the fact that lowering one room's price doesn't just increase its demand—it steals demand from other rooms in the same hotel. Without modeling intra-hotel substitution, pricing optimization fails: you might lower a room's price expecting it to sell more, but the incremental revenue is eaten by losing sales of higher-margin rooms.
1229.ap: BFSNet models the two-stage booking funnel explicitly: first, predicting whether a user will click a hotel; second, predicting whether they'll convert within that hotel. To capture substitution effects, it uses a mixing network that incorporates economic theory—specifically, monotonic substitution relationships. The idea is that if price of room A goes up, demand for similar room B goes up (people substitute toward B), but with a well-behaved mathematical relationship, not chaotic jumps.
1229.ww: Separating the funnel stages lets the model learn hotel-click and within-hotel conversion patterns independently, which is more interpretable. The mixing network, grounded in economic theory, ensures that learned substitution relationships are realistic (price changes produce smooth, monotonic demand shifts, not paradoxes).
1229.po: On benchmarks, BFSNet delivers more accurate demand predictions than collapsed single-stage models, especially when substitution effects are strong. This translates to better revenue management: pricing recommendations account for real consumer choices, avoiding the costly errors of ignoring substitution effects.
